source: AI-generated original. Common Test-style practice; no exam text reproduced.
passageHtml:
Useful Friction: Why Easier Is Not Always Better

Designers often try to remove every delay from daily life. Doors open automatically, applications remember our choices, and online stores allow purchases with one click. These changes save time. Yet researchers have begun to examine situations in which a small amount of difficulty - sometimes called useful friction - can improve judgment, memory, or safety.

Consider digital reading. When information appears in a smooth, endless stream, people may continue scrolling without deciding what matters. A short pause between sections can encourage readers to predict what comes next or summarize what they have just learned. The pause does not add new information; it changes how actively the reader processes what is already there.

Useful friction can also protect people from impulsive action. Some banks allow customers to place a twenty-four-hour delay on unusually large transfers. The delay may feel inconvenient, but it gives users time to notice fraud or reconsider an emotional purchase. Similarly, a confirmation screen that clearly states the amount and recipient can prevent errors better than a tiny warning message that users automatically ignore.

However, difficulty is not automatically useful. A complicated medical form may prevent patients from receiving care, and an unclear station sign may cause travelers to miss trains. The key question is whether the extra effort supports the user's goal or merely blocks it. Good friction is targeted: it slows down a risky decision but does not make ordinary tasks unnecessarily hard.

Researchers in a university learning lab tested this distinction. One group of students watched a twelve-minute video without interruption. A second group saw three brief prompts asking them to choose the best summary of the previous section. A third group experienced random pauses containing no question. The summary-prompt group remembered the most information one week later. The random-pause group reported the greatest annoyance and performed no better than the uninterrupted group.

ConditionAverage recall after one weekReported annoyance (1-5)
No interruption61%1.8
Summary prompts76%2.4
Random pauses60%4.1

These findings suggest that designers should not ask only, “Can we make this faster?” They should also ask, “At which moment would a deliberate pause help the user think?” In education, finance, and public safety, the best design may be neither perfectly smooth nor frustratingly difficult. It may contain just enough resistance to support a better decision.

Presentation Slides

  1. Definition: a small, purposeful difficulty
  2. Possible benefits: deeper processing; fewer impulsive errors
  3. Important distinction: targeted friction vs. pointless obstacles
  4. Study result: summary prompts improved later recall
  5. Discussion: Where would a useful pause improve your daily routine?

Further Examples

Useful friction appears in physical environments as well. A brightly colored strip before a staircase may make walkers slow down and notice a change in height. A tool cabinet with outlines showing where each item belongs makes returning equipment slightly more deliberate, but it also makes missing tools immediately visible. In both cases, the design interrupts automatic behavior at the exact moment attention is valuable.

There is also an ethical issue. Designers have the power to decide where users encounter delay. A company could add many steps to cancel a subscription while keeping enrollment effortless. That is friction, but it serves the company rather than the user. Researchers therefore argue that useful friction should be transparent and proportionate. Users should understand why a pause exists, and the effort required should match the seriousness of the decision.

In classrooms, teachers can apply this idea without making lessons unpleasant. Asking students to retrieve an answer before showing it, compare two possible explanations, or write a one-sentence summary introduces a small challenge. The challenge is useful only when students have enough knowledge to respond. If the task is far beyond their current understanding, the result is confusion rather than deeper learning.

questions.question: What does “useful friction” mean in the passage?
options: A technical problem that always slows users
A purposeful difficulty that can support better thinking or safety
Any design feature that makes a service expensive
A random interruption used to test patience
questions.answer: A purposeful difficulty that can support better thinking or safety
questions.evidence: a small amount of difficulty ... can improve judgment, memory, or safety
questions.reason_ja: 思考・記憶・安全を助ける意図的な小さな負荷です。

questions.question: Why can a pause help digital readers?
options: It adds information not contained in the text.
It forces them to purchase the next section.
It may encourage active prediction or summary.
It makes the screen physically brighter.
questions.answer: It may encourage active prediction or summary.
questions.evidence: encourage readers to predict ... or summarize
questions.reason_ja: 予測や要約を促し、能動的処理につながります。

questions.question: Which example shows friction used mainly for safety?
options: An endless social media feed
A delay on a large bank transfer
An unclear medical form
A random pause in a video
questions.answer: A delay on a large bank transfer
questions.evidence: gives users time to notice fraud
questions.reason_ja: 詐欺や衝動的送金を防ぐための遅延です。

questions.question: What distinction does the author emphasize?
options: All inconvenience improves memory.
Useful friction supports a goal, while bad difficulty merely obstructs it.
Fast systems are always unsafe.
Public services should avoid confirmation screens.
questions.answer: Useful friction supports a goal, while bad difficulty merely obstructs it.
questions.evidence: whether the extra effort supports the user's goal or merely blocks it
questions.reason_ja: 目的を助ける負荷と、単なる障害を区別しています。

questions.question: What can be concluded from the study table?
options: Random pauses produced the highest recall.
Summary prompts improved recall with only a moderate rise in annoyance.
No interruption caused the greatest annoyance.
All three conditions produced nearly identical results.
questions.answer: Summary prompts improved recall with only a moderate rise in annoyance.
questions.reason_ja: 要約プロンプトは記憶を高め、苛立ちはランダム停止よりかなり低いです。

questions.question: Which student habit is most likely to apply the article effectively?
options: Adding random alarms while reading
Pausing after each section to state its main point
Making every routine task more complicated
Removing all confirmation screens from payments
questions.answer: Pausing after each section to state its main point
questions.reason_ja: 各区切りで要点を言う行動が研究結果に合います。
